A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same title, authors and central framework. All 12 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2, including v2's appendices A–D, are readable. Much appendix material matches content previously in the main text.

before.justification: v1 presents formal and normative arguments, illustrated by incidents reconstructed from cited reports. It does not report original experiments, participant observations or a distinct empirical data-analysis study.

after.justification: Appendix C.1 reports original qualitative observations from one author's ethics consultations and workshops, including recurring patterns in practitioners' understanding of sociotechnical failures and their allocation of responsibility.

M1.justification: The three HITL configurations, emergency-stop behavior and human–machine interaction procedures are retained. Revised formal definitions and expanded explanations do not introduce a new operational algorithm, architecture or training/inference procedure.

E1.justification: Neither version introduces training or evaluation datasets or task benchmarks. The existing illustrative applications and failure cases remain. The consultations newly described in Appendix C.1 explain the existing taxonomy's development rather than introduce an additional evaluation scenario.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing algorithms or baseline systems. Expanded comparisons with published taxonomies and oversight research are related-work discussions, not baseline evaluations.

E3.justification: No revised evaluation metrics, splits, budgets, controls or testing procedures are reported. The newly disclosed consultation dates, participant coverage and workshop format document the taxonomy's provenance; they do not establish a changed experimental protocol.

E4.justification: The MCG, Notre-Dame and Uber case studies are retained, with the first two relocated to Appendix C. Appendix C.2 extends the MCG failure analysis with follow-up evidence that flagged attendees did not receive metal-detecting wand checks. No ablation or robustness experiment is added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or statistical uncertainty estimates. The new consultation account is qualitative; the discussion of random oracle machines is theoretical.

E6.justification: Appendix C.1 newly reports practitioners' stronger understanding of technical failures and tendency to disclaim responsibility for sociotechnical failures. Table 1 expands the detailed failure inventory while retaining the five categories. Appendix C.2 adds omitted wand checks and subsequent convictions to the MCG account; the existing accident timings and principal conclusions remain.

T1.justification: v1 defines a real query using a computational fork and more than one possible downstream output. v2 instead requires that branches have different sets of possible outputs, a substantive tightening. Appendix B.3 adds an integer-parity example demonstrating dependence on preceding queries. The underlying oracle, many-one and Turing reduction framework remains.

C1.justification: The abstracts and conclusions retain the same principal contributions: computational characterization of HITL, a failure taxonomy, legal implications and an explainability–responsibility trade-off. The six design and regulatory recommendations also retain their meaning.

C2.justification: v1's discussion links stronger interaction to reduced predictability and lost explainability. v2 Sections 2.2 and 4.3 more clearly distinguish visibility of intermediate steps from attribution of causal responsibility. Appendix B.1 substantially qualifies the human-as-oracle interpretation. Appendices D.1–D.4 add GDPR exceptions and guidance, a SCHUFA automation-bias analysis, and qualifications concerning mesothelioma liability and the Compensation Act 2006.

D1.justification: The new reproducibility statement and Appendix C.1 disclose consultations during 2020–2022 with over 25 AI startups, workshops with three additional companies and the author's advisory role. v2 also discloses LLM assistance for literature search and editing. These are limited provenance additions; no consultation corpus or detailed analysis protocol is supplied.

R1.justification: The literature grounding expands substantively across several areas: harm and safety in Appendix A.1, computability of ethical decisions in B.1, category-specific empirical failure research in C.1, and regulatory guidance and liability critiques in Appendix D. Examples include newly cited work by Diberardino et al., Moor, Bellaby, Tsai et al. and Morgan, plus ICO guidance.

P1.justification: v2 extensively condenses and rewrites the main narrative, adds numbered sections and cross-references, standardizes machine/ADMS terminology, and redistributes substantial existing exposition into appendices A–D. The introduction and legal discussion are substantially reorganized, beyond the addition of new content.

P2.justification: The two-column, text-only presentation becomes a single-column layout. New Figure 1 diagrams the three HITL configurations, Figure 2 illustrates computational transparency, and Table 1 presents an expanded five-column failure inventory. These are substantial changes to visual explanation and document layout.

improvement.justification: The tighter real-query definition and clearer separation of intermediate transparency from causal responsibility improve precision relative to v1. Consultation provenance, legal qualifications and explanatory diagrams also make the argument easier to assess. The consultation account remains informal, and the universal trade-off remains an argument rather than an established formal result, limiting the overall gain.
